title: Fish Loaves Mosaic
subject: Contracts
stem:
Before Mary laid a tile, Timothy, Peter’s choir friend and an avid collector of Christian art, said in front of both Peter and Mary that he would not approve Mary’s sketch. That rejection mattered because Peter and Mary had already signed a detailed writing: Mary would cover the side of Peter’s privately owned vintage camper with a fish-and-loaves mosaic according to Mary’s attached sketch, and Peter would pay $18,000 at completion. Peter’s sister Ruth was not a party to the agreement and owned no interest in the camper. At Peter’s insistence, the writing said that neither party would be bound unless Timothy approved Mary’s sketch. After Timothy rejected the sketch, Peter nevertheless told Mary to go ahead with the mosaic. Mary reluctantly began and completed 45% of the work. Peter then repudiated any duty to pay the contract price or any part of it.

If Mary now sues Peter for damages for breach of contract, which concept best supports Mary’s claim?
call: If Mary now sues Peter for damages for breach of contract, which concept best supports Mary's claim?
rightExplanation: B is correct. Peter’s duty to pay was tied to Timothy’s approval, but Peter chose to go forward after Timothy rejected the sketch. That conduct waived the approval condition. Mary then materially relied on that waiver by completing 45% of the mosaic. Gold Key: a protected party who orders performance after an express condition fails has waived the condition, and after material reliance the waiver cannot be revoked. Silver Key: lock the call before the labels: this is a breach-of-contract claim on a signed writing, so the contract-lane concept beats backup recovery labels.

c3.label: CUT A — Promissory estoppel
c3.text: The call asks for a concept supporting a breach-of-contract claim. A signed writing is already on the page. Promissory estoppel is a neighboring reliance concept, but it is not the best lane when the contract lane is open.

c3.label: CUT C — Unjust enrichment
c3.text: The choice answers the fairness question: “Should Peter keep the benefit without paying?” The call is narrower: “What contract concept supports Mary’s breach claim?” That makes C not responsive.

c3.label: CUT D — Substantial performance
c3.text: The choice points to the amount of work completed. The stem points to a failed approval condition followed by an order to proceed. The better concept is waiver of the condition, not substantial completion.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: B remains. It matches the stem’s three-part trigger: failed condition, order to proceed, reliance.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: Not needed. The CUT leaves one residual.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Anchor-assisted call only: apply the Gold Key for waiver of condition after reliance.

studentScript: Signed writing. Approval failed. Peter said proceed. Mary relied. Backup labels are wrong lane. Pick irrevocable waiver of condition.

A.signal: The call says breach of contract and the stem gives a detailed writing.
A.lawyer: Promissory estoppel is not the best theory where an actual contract claim is available and the rule issue is waiver of condition.

B.signal: The answer names the condition event that the stem keeps repeating.
B.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 84 and 246 support waiver/excuse of condition after conduct and reliance.

C.signal: The answer tracks benefit received, not the contract concept assigned by the call.
C.lawyer: Unjust enrichment is not the best support for a breach claim when a valid contract supplies the duty.

D.signal: The stem's decisive facts are condition failure and order to proceed, not completion level.
D.lawyer: Substantial performance is a constructive-condition performance doctrine; this item turns on waiver of an express condition.

goldKeys.statement: A party protected by an express condition can waive that condition by ordering performance after the condition fails; after the other party materially relies, the waiver cannot be revoked.
goldKeys.trigger: Approval condition fails; protected party says proceed; performing party completes a meaningful part of the work.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 84, 246; Clark v. West, 193 N.Y. 349, 86 N.E. 1 (1908).

silverKeys.statement: Lock the call before the labels: the question asks for the concept supporting a breach-of-contract claim, so backup recovery labels move behind the contract-lane answer unless the contract lane is blocked.
silverKeys.trigger: A signed writing plus a call asking for damages for breach of contract.
silverKeys.unlocks: Promissory-estoppel and unjust-enrichment bait when a signed contract is on the page.

remediation.title: Contract lane before backup remedy lane
remediation.signal: The call says breach of contract and the stem gives a signed writing.
remediation.studentMove: Cut promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment unless the contract lane is blocked.
remediation.tinyRule: Use waiver when the protected party gives up a failed condition and the other side relies.
remediation.trap: Choosing the fairest-sounding payment theory instead of the contract concept.
